body: Hi. For the next ninety days, a small daily note will help you become someone who keeps in touch with the people who matter, through messages, calls and the occasional letter.
Keeping in touch is less about grand gestures and more about small, regular reminders that someone is in your thoughts.
Today, write down five people you would like to hear from more often. These are your first threads to tend.
Send one short message today that needs no reply: Saw this and thought of you.
Many friendships fade not because of conflict but because no one reaches out first. You can be the one who does.
Pick a regular time each week for keeping in touch, such as Sunday afternoon. Habits like a home.
You do not need a reason to get in touch. Just because is a perfectly good reason.
Notice the guilt about having left it too long. Let it go. A late message is far better than no message.
Write a short note to someone who helped you in the past. Tell them one specific thing you remember.
Keep a list of birthdays and important dates in one place. Remembering them is a simple way to show care.
Try a voice note instead of a text today. Hearing a familiar voice often means more than reading words.
Buy a few cards or a pack of postcards. Having them ready makes it easier to send one on impulse.
Share a photo of something you did this week with someone far away. Small windows into your life keep closeness alive.
Ask a friend a specific question in your next message: How did the interview go? Specific questions show you remember.
It is fine if some people do not reply quickly. Keeping in touch is about offering connection, not keeping score.
Write a real letter by hand this week. It does not have to be long; a page is a gift.
When a friend comes to mind, act on it within the day. That small impulse is worth following.
Call an older relative for ten minutes. Many people treasure a call more than they say.
Notice which friends you only see on social media. Choose one to message directly instead.
If you feel awkward reaching out after a long gap, simply say so: It has been ages, and I have missed you.
Send a message celebrating someone else's good news. Shared joy strengthens bonds.
Keep a running note of things friends mention: a new job, a sick pet, an upcoming trip. Follow up later.
Try arranging a regular catch-up with one friend, such as a monthly call. Rhythms make keeping in touch easier.
Write to someone you have lost touch with because of a move. Distance does not have to mean disconnection.
Today, reply to a message you have been meaning to answer. Clearing the backlog lightens the mind.
Think about how you like to be kept in touch with. Others may like the same: a call, a card, a funny link.
If a friend is going through something hard, check in again a week later. Second check-ins mean a lot.
Write a thank-you note for a recent kindness. Gratitude in writing lasts longer than gratitude in passing.
Notice the people who always reach out to you first. This week, be the one who starts.
Send a postcard from somewhere you visit, even if it is close to home. Postcards are small pieces of shared experience.
Keep in touch with a former colleague you liked. Work friendships can last well beyond the job.
Make a short video message for someone's birthday. Effort shows care more than polish does.
Choose one friend to write a longer message to this week, sharing what has been on your mind.
Remember that keeping in touch includes listening. Ask how people are and let them answer fully.
If you lose momentum, start again with a single message. There is no streak to break.
Write down a memory you share with an old friend and send it to them. Memories are good conversation starters.
Notice how you feel after reaching out. Often there is a warmth that makes the next message easier.
Plan to see someone in person this month if you can. Messages keep threads alive; meetings strengthen them.
Ask a friend for a recommendation: a book, a recipe, a show. It invites a reply and a follow-up chat.
Write to a teacher, mentor or coach who made a difference. They rarely hear how their work turned out.
Mark a friend's small milestone, such as a first week in a new job, with a quick note. Small milestones are often forgotten.
Keep a small stash of stamps at home. Removing small obstacles makes letter-writing more likely.
Send a message to someone who is new to your area or workplace. Reaching out to newcomers is a lovely habit.
Notice who might feel lonely right now. A simple message can brighten their week.
Halfway through. How many threads have you picked back up since you began?
Share something you are learning or enjoying with a friend who would appreciate it.
If a friend's reply is short, do not take it personally. People are often busy or tired.
Write a note to a family member you see often but rarely talk to deeply.
Arrange a video call with friends in different places. A shared screen can feel like a shared table.
Notice that keeping in touch is a skill you are practising. It becomes easier with time.
Send a message to a neighbour or someone in your local community. Connection close to home matters too.
Write down three things you appreciate about a friend and tell them one of them.
If someone has reached out to you recently, thank them for thinking of you.
Try writing a letter to a friend's child or a younger relative. Children often love getting post.
Remember anniversaries of loss for friends who are grieving. A gentle message on a hard day is deeply kind.
Keep your messages honest. You do not need to present only the highlights of your life.
Reconnect with someone from a hobby, club or class you used to attend.
Notice which forms of contact feel most natural to you, and lean into them.
Plan a small surprise for a friend: a card arriving on an ordinary day.
If you feel shy about writing, start with just two lines. Short is still sweet.
Write to a friend about a song, film or place that reminds you of them.
Send a quick message of encouragement to someone facing a challenge this week.
Notice the friendships that have grown warmer since you began reaching out more.
Try a shared activity at a distance: watching the same film, reading the same book, cooking the same meal.
Ask an older friend or relative to tell you a story from their past. People love to be asked.
Keep a contact list of people you want to stay close to, and look at it once a week.
If you move, change jobs or have news, tell your people directly instead of letting them find out online.
Write a letter you might never send, to someone you have lost touch with. It can help you decide whether to reach out.
Notice when a friend is quieter than usual. A gentle How are you really? can open a door.
Remember that keeping in touch goes both ways, but someone has to go first. You can be the steady one.
Send a funny memory or old photo to a group of friends. Laughter brings people together.
Practise ending calls with a plan: Let's talk again next month. It gives the next contact a place to land.
Write a few lines to someone you admire but do not know well. Appreciation is rarely unwelcome.
Notice how keeping in touch affects your own mood. Connection tends to feed both people.
If someone has drifted away despite your efforts, it is fine to let them go with kindness.
Reach out to someone you have been avoiding because of a small misunderstanding. A warm message can clear the air.
Choose one friendship to invest in a little more over the coming months.
Write a note to yourself about the kind of friend and relative you want to be.
Send a message to a friend telling them what their friendship means to you.
Plan a reunion, big or small, with people you have not seen together in years.
Notice how many people now hear from you regularly. That is a quiet network of care you built.
Keep the habits that worked best: the weekly slot, the stash of cards, the follow-up notes.
Write one last handwritten letter this month, to someone who would treasure it.
You have learned that keeping in touch does not need perfect timing, just a little attention.
Think of someone who might not expect to hear from you. Surprise them with a kind message.
Look back at your list of five people. How have those threads changed?
Notice one relationship that is stronger today because you reached out.
Keeping in touch is a way of saying you matter to me, again and again.
Look back over these weeks. Which message or letter meant the most to send?
Remember that you can keep reaching out long after these notes end.
You started by naming five people. Now you have a habit that can hold many more.
This is the last note. You have become someone who keeps in touch, and the people in your life are richer for it.
